text:
Most relevant lightweight lead: [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) constructs a directed, weighted item graph from interaction histories and purchase order, supporting neighborhood-based recommendation without pretrained representations. Useful inspiration for a sparse transition branch alongside SASRec; its complementarity interpretation remains a behavioral proxy, not proof of functional compatibility. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02130) models complementary relationships through both relevance and dissimilarity, using low-pass and mid-pass graph filters with attention. Key lesson: similarity-only aggregation can erase distinctions useful for complementary recommendations.

Recent metadata approaches often violate the available-data constraints. [KGSCL (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089360802500070X) uses explicit Amazon substitution/complement relations for sequence augmentation; those relations are unavailable here. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines SASRec-style modeling with BERT-encoded titles, descriptions and reviews, requiring modification to remove pretrained weights and reviews. [MMSC (2025; revised 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22268) emphasizes that behavioral associations provide noisy supervision, but uses a multimodal foundation model and LLM-assisted supervision.

Constraint-compatible research direction, inferred from these papers: retain separate directed transition and symmetric text-similarity channels; encode titles/descriptions with randomly initialized token embeddings and pooling, then learn gated fusion with item IDs through next-item prediction. Treat channels as transition and content evidence rather than assigning unsupported complement/substitute labels. Compare against unchanged SASRec using the pinned macro validation HR@10; published results on different recommendation tasks do not establish gains for this benchmark.
